reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Endocrine Society clinical guidance
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder from severe biallelic INSR (insulin receptor) mutations causing the most extreme form of genetic insulin resistance
Presents in infancy with intrauterine and postnatal growth failure, marked subcutaneous fat and muscle loss, and dysmorphic 'elfin' facies
Acanthosis nigricans, hypertrichosis, and enlarged genitalia are characteristic, and girls may show ovarian cysts and virilisation
The hallmark glucose pattern is fasting hypoglycaemia alternating with severe postprandial hyperglycaemia, reflecting near-absent insulin signalling
Circulating insulin levels are enormously elevated because target tissues cannot respond to insulin
Because the defect is at the receptor, leptin has a limited role and recombinant IGF-1 (and IGF-1/IGFBP-3) is used to engage the IGF-1 receptor and improve metabolic control
It is the most severe end of the INSR spectrum, more extreme than Rabson-Mendenhall syndrome and type A insulin resistance
Diagnosis rests on the phenotype, extreme hyperinsulinaemia with the fasting-hypoglycaemia/postprandial-hyperglycaemia pattern, and INSR genetics
reference.pathophysiology: Donohue syndrome results from severe loss-of-function mutations in both copies of the insulin receptor gene (INSR), so insulin can bind but cannot transmit its signal. Insulin normally suppresses hepatic glucose output and promotes tissue glucose uptake and growth; when receptor signalling is almost absent, tissues cannot use glucose or grow normally despite grossly elevated insulin concentrations. This produces intrauterine growth restriction, near-total loss of adipose tissue and muscle, and a paradoxical glucose profile of fasting hypoglycaemia (from insulin's residual and IGF-mediated effects and poor counter-regulation) with severe postprandial hyperglycaemia. Impaired insulin/IGF signalling also underlies the dysmorphism, hypertrichosis, and organ abnormalities.
additionalDifferentials: Other neonatal progeroid or growth-restriction syndromes
Intrauterine growth restriction from placental causes
Congenital infections causing dysmorphism and growth failure
additionalInvestigations: Fasting and postprandial glucose to capture the hypoglycaemia/hyperglycaemia pattern
Fasting insulin and C-peptide, characteristically extremely elevated
INSR gene sequencing to confirm biallelic mutations
Serum leptin and lipid profile to characterise the metabolic state
Pelvic/gonadal imaging for ovarian cysts or genital abnormalities
Growth and developmental assessment with review of antenatal growth
redFlags: Recurrent fasting or nocturnal hypoglycaemia in infancy
Severe failure to thrive with progressive wasting
Life-threatening infections given frequent early mortality
Marked postprandial hyperglycaemia with ketosis risk
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is poor, with most affected infants dying within the first one to two years of life from metabolic instability and infection, although recombinant IGF-1-based therapy may modestly improve metabolic control and survival in some children.
pitfalls: Misreading the extreme hyperinsulinaemia as an insulinoma rather than receptor resistance
Attempting to control hyperglycaemia with escalating insulin, which is ineffective
Failing to arrange INSR genetics and genetic counselling for the family
Confusing the elfin dysmorphism with a congenital infection
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guidance on severe insulin resistance
